blocks.text: Long ago, a king named Acrisius was told a terrible thing. "One day," said a prophet, "your daughter Danae will have a son, and that son will cause your death."

Acrisius was frightened, and he was cruel. He locked Danae away under the ground, in a room lined with brass, so that no one could ever come near her. But the gods cannot be tricked so easily. Danae had a baby boy anyway, and his face shone like the morning star. She named him Perseus.
When King Acrisius found out, he put Danae and her baby in a big wooden chest and pushed it out to sea.

The chest floated on the waves for days and nights. Danae sang to her baby, and the baby slept. At last the chest bumped against the rocks of an island called Seriphos. A kind old fisherman named Dictys was there with his net. He lifted them out of the chest.
"You will be a daughter to me," he said to Danae, "and this baby will be my grandson." And so they lived with Dictys and his wife for fifteen happy years.

Perseus grew up tall and strong. But Dictys had a brother, King Polydectes, who was greedy and cruel. He wanted to marry Danae, and she did not want to marry him. So he made a plan to get rid of Perseus.
The king held a great feast. Every guest brought him a present: a horse, a ring, a sword. Perseus was a poor sailor boy, and he had nothing to give.
"Where is your present, Perseus?" sneered the king. All the guests laughed.
Perseus turned red. "I'll bring you a better present than all of these!" he shouted. "I'll bring you the head of Medusa the Gorgon!"
Everyone laughed even louder. Medusa was a monster with snakes for hair. Anyone who looked at her face turned to stone.
"Then go," said the king, "and don't come back without it."
Perseus went down to the cliffs, feeling foolish. "I spoke too fast," he said. "But I will keep my promise, if the gods will help me."
Then a bright white cloud came floating over the sea. Out of it stepped the goddess Athena, with a shining brass shield, and Hermes, the messenger of the gods, with wings on his sandals.
"We will help you," said Athena. "Take my shield. Never look at Medusa herself, only at her reflection in the shield, and you will be safe."
"Take my sandals," said Hermes. "They will carry you over land and sea like a bird. And take my sword. It is so sharp that you will only need to strike once."
Perseus put on the winged sandals, took a deep breath, and jumped off the cliff. Instead of falling, he flew.

First he flew far to the north, to a land of ice and snow. There lived the three Gray Sisters, three very old women who had only one eye and one tooth to share between them. They passed the eye from hand to hand. Perseus crept up, and when one sister held out the eye to pass it, he took it.
"Give it back!" the sisters screeched.
"I will," said Perseus, "when you tell me the way to Medusa."
So they told him: "Go south, to the giant Atlas." Perseus gave back their eye and flew away.

He flew south, over sparkling seas, until he came to a beautiful garden where nymphs danced around a tree of golden apples. Above them on a mountain knelt the giant Atlas, holding up the sky on his shoulders.

"I can see the Gorgons' island from up here," said Atlas. "But to get close, you'll need the Cap of Darkness, which makes you invisible. My nieces will fetch it for you. But promise me one thing. When you have Medusa's head, show it to me. I am so tired of holding up the sky. I want to turn to stone and rest."
Perseus promised. One of the nymphs went deep down into the earth and came back with the Cap of Darkness. Perseus put it on and vanished.

Then he flew on, to a strange, gray island at the edge of the world. There he heard the rustle of great wings. The three Gorgons lay asleep on the rocks. They had brass claws and golden wings. Two of them were ugly and fierce. The third was Medusa. Her face looked almost sad, but on her head the snakes wriggled and hissed.
Perseus did not look at her. He held up the shiny shield and looked only at the picture in it. He flew down, very quietly, keeping his eyes on the shield. Then he swung Hermes's sword, just once.

He wrapped Medusa's head in a goatskin bag, without looking at it, and flew away as fast as he could. The other two Gorgons woke up, screaming. They flew after him, flapping and howling. But the winged sandals were faster, and by nightfall the Gorgons were only two black specks far behind.

Perseus kept his promise to Atlas. He held up the Gorgon's head, and the tired giant turned into a great stone mountain, which still holds up the sky today. The mountains are called the Atlas Mountains.
On his way home, a storm blew Perseus off course, over the hot desert. At last he came to a rocky seashore. Chained to a rock at the edge of the water was a young woman.
"Who are you?" asked Perseus, taking off his cap so she could see him. "Why are you chained up here?"

"I am Princess Andromeda," she said, crying. "My mother boasted that I was more beautiful than the sea nymphs. That made the sea gods angry. They sent a sea monster to wreck our land. The only way to stop it is to give me to the monster. And here it comes."
Perseus cut her chains with his sword. Then a huge black shape came swimming toward the shore, with waves foaming around it.

"Hide your eyes," said Perseus. He flew up high, and then he swooped down like a shooting star. He held up the Gorgon's head. When Andromeda looked again, the monster was gone. In its place was a long black rock in the water.

Andromeda's mother and father were overjoyed. Perseus and Andromeda were married, and there was a feast that lasted seven days. When Andromeda's old uncle came with his soldiers to stop the wedding, Perseus showed them the Gorgon's head too, and they turned to stone.

That night, Athena came to Perseus in a dream. "You have done well," she said. "Now give back the sword, the sandals and the cap, so I can return them to their owners." When Perseus woke up, they were gone.
At last Perseus sailed home to Seriphos with Andromeda. He hugged his mother and the kind old fisherman, Dictys. Then he went to the hall of King Polydectes, who was feasting with his friends.
"So, you're back," sneered the king. "Where's my present?"

"Here it is," said Perseus. He took the Gorgon's head out of the bag. The king and all his unkind guests turned to stone, right there at the table. People say they are still sitting there on the hillside, a circle of gray stones.
Perseus made good old Dictys the king of Seriphos. Then he gave Medusa's head to Athena, and she put it on the front of her shield.

Perseus wanted to make peace with his grandfather, King Acrisius. He found him watching some games in a faraway town. Perseus joined the games without telling anyone his name. He won the running, the jumping and the wrestling. Then he threw a heavy discus. But a gust of wind caught it. It flew sideways and struck old Acrisius on the foot, and the old king fell down and died. The prophecy had come true after all, just as the gods had said, even though Perseus never meant any harm.

Perseus was very sorry. He went home and became a good king. He and Andromeda had seven children and lived to be very old. And when their lives were over, Athena lifted them up into the sky. On a clear night you can still see them among the stars: Perseus holding the Gorgon's head, Andromeda with her arms spread wide, and her mother and father close by.
A simplified retelling of Charles Kingsley's “Perseus” in The Heroes, or Greek Fairy Tales for My Children (1856). The original is listed under Other versions.
